## Alternative proofs

### logic:hennessy-milner — Game-theoretic (back-and-forth) proof

**Idea.** Instead of building the relation $Z$ of modal equivalence and checking the zigzag conditions by a compactness-style argument with finite conjunctions, phrase the failure of bisimilarity as a finite game: Spoiler moves in one model, Duplicator answers in the other. On image-finite models, if Duplicator has no winning strategy from $(w,w')$, then some finite play already exposes the mismatch, and that finite play can be converted into a single modal formula of degree equal to its length that holds at one point and fails at the other. This makes explicit where image-finiteness enters (Spoiler has only finitely many moves at each turn, so a failed defence is detected after finitely many rounds).

1. Step 1 — Short Claim: Define the bisimulation game from $(v,v')$: Spoiler moves along $R$ or $R'$, Duplicator must answer along the other relation to a pair again in the game; Duplicator wins infinite plays, Spoiler wins if Duplicator cannot answer. (definition)
2. Step 2 — Short Claim: Duplicator has a winning strategy from $(w,w')$ iff $\mathcal{M},w\mathrel{\underline{\leftrightarrow}}\mathcal{M}',w'$. (the set of pairs from which Duplicator can defend is exactly the greatest bisimulation; verify atomic harmony, forth and back)
3. Step 3 — Short Claim: If Duplicator has no winning strategy from $(v,v')$, then Spoiler wins within $n$ rounds for some $n$, and then $v$ and $v'$ disagree on some formula of modal degree $\le n$. (induction on $n$: at a position where Duplicator cannot defend, either atomic harmony fails, giving a propositional variable, or some move of Spoiler has no answer, and by image-finiteness the finitely many candidate answers $u'_{1},\dots,u'_{k}$ each fail within $n-1$ rounds, so the conjunction $C_{1}\wedge\cdots\wedge C_{k}$ of the corresponding separating formulas gives $\Diamond(C_{1}\wedge\cdots\wedge C_{k})$)
4. Step 4 — Short Claim: Hence modal equivalence of $w$ and $w'$ forces Duplicator to have a winning strategy, i.e. bisimilarity. (contrapositive of Step 3 together with Step 2)

**Prerequisites.** Definition of bisimulation; the finiteness of the set of successors (image-finiteness) used in Step 3 to take a finite conjunction; determinacy of finite games is not needed, only the explicit strategy analysis.

**Why instructive.** It isolates the exact role of image-finiteness (finitely many answers to combine into one formula) and shows that the Hennessy-Milner theorem is the finite-approximation shadow of the game characterization of bisimilarity, which is the standard tool in concurrency theory.

### logic:finite-tree-model — Pruning the unravelling

**Idea.** Start from the tree unravelling $\mathcal{M}^{\to}_{w}$ of a model satisfying $A$ (which is bisimilar to $\mathcal{M},w$ by logic:unravelling-bisimilar) and cut it down: keep only the nodes needed as witnesses for the boxed subformulas of $A$ that are false along the branch, and stop at depth $d(A)$. This gives the same finite tree but obtained by selection inside an already constructed (possibly infinite) tree rather than by building the tree top-down.

1. Step 1 — Short Claim: $\mathcal{M}^{\to}_{w},(w)\models A$, and the unravelling is a tree with root $(w)$. (logic:unravelling-bisimilar)
2. Step 2 — Short Claim: For every node $s$ of the unravelling with $\mathrm{last}(s)=u$ and every $\Box B\in\mathrm{Sub}(A)$ with $d(\Box B)\le d(A)-\mathrm{depth}(s)$ and $\mathcal{M},u\not\models\Box B$, there is a child $t$ of $s$ with $\mathcal{M},\mathrm{last}(t)\not\models B$. (truth definition plus the fact that children of $s$ correspond to all $R$-successors of $u$)
3. Step 3 — Short Claim: The subtree $\mathcal{T}$ consisting of the root, of all nodes of depth $\le d(A)$, and of one chosen witness child for each false boxed subformula at each retained node, is finite, of depth $\le d(A)$, with at most $k$ children per node. (finitely many choices at each of finitely many nodes)
4. Step 4 — Short Claim: For every retained node $s$ and every $B\in\mathrm{Sub}(A)$ with $d(B)\le d(A)-\mathrm{depth}(s)$, $\mathcal{T},s\models B\iff\mathcal{M},\mathrm{last}(s)\models B$; in particular $\mathcal{T},(w)\models A$. (induction on $B$ as in the given Step 2, using that all children of a retained node are $R^{\to}$-successors and that witnesses were kept)

**Prerequisites.** The unravelling and its bisimulation invariance (logic:unravelling, logic:unravelling-bisimilar), which come after the definition of bisimulation but before this theorem on the page; otherwise the same tools as the given proof.

**Why instructive.** It separates the two ingredients of the finite tree model property: bisimulation-invariance (why the unravelling may replace the original model) and the selection of finitely many witnesses (why depth and branching can be bounded). It also explains why the construction does not preserve frame conditions, since the unravelling never does.

## Alternative definitions

### logic:bisimulation (equivalent)

A bisimulation between $\mathcal{M}$ and $\mathcal{M}'$ is a relation $Z$ such that $Z\subseteq Z_{0}$, $Z\circ R\subseteq R'\circ Z$ and $Z^{-1}\circ R'\subseteq R\circ Z$, where $Z_{0}=\{(w,w'):w,w'\text{ agree on all propositional variables}\}$ and $\circ$ denotes relational composition.

**Conditions.** Same setting (two Kripke models, arbitrary relations); no extra hypotheses.

**Equivalence.** $Z\circ R\subseteq R'\circ Z$ says: whenever $wZv$ and $wRw_{1}$ there is $w'_{1}$ with $w'R'w'_{1}$ and $w_{1}Zw'_{1}$, i.e. the forth condition. Similarly $Z^{-1}\circ R'\subseteq R\circ Z$ is the back condition, and $Z\subseteq Z_{0}$ is atomic harmony.

**Reference.** Blackburn, de Rijke, Venema, Modal Logic (Chapter 2); Sangiorgi, Introduction to Bisimulation and Coinduction.

### logic:bisimulation (equivalent)

Bisimilarity $\mathrel{\underline{\leftrightarrow}}$ is the union of all bisimulations, equivalently the greatest fixed point of the monotone operator $F(Z)=Z_{0}\cap\{(w,w'):\forall v\,(wRv\Rightarrow\exists v'\,(w'R'v'\wedge vZv'))\text{ and dually}\}$ on relations.

**Conditions.** Same setting; the greatest fixed point exists by Knaster-Tarski since $F$ is monotone on the complete lattice of relations.

**Equivalence.** Any bisimulation is a post-fixed point of $F$ ($Z\subseteq F(Z)$), and the union of post-fixed points is again one, hence the largest; on image-finite models it is also the limit of the decreasing sequence $Z_{0}\supseteq Z_{1}\supseteq\cdots$ where $Z_{i+1}=F(Z_{i})$, which is exactly $n$-bisimilarity at stage $i$.

**Reference.** Blackburn, de Rijke, Venema, Modal Logic (Chapter 2); Davoren and Goré, 'Bisimulations generated from non-deterministic repetitions' (for the fixed-point view).

### logic:bounded-morphism (equivalent)

A bounded morphism is a map $f\colon W\to W'$ whose graph is a bisimulation and which is total (defined on all of $W$).

**Conditions.** Same setting; totality of $f$ is required, otherwise one gets a partial bounded morphism (a bisimulation that is a partial function).

**Equivalence.** If the graph of $f$ is a bisimulation, atomic harmony gives condition 1, the forth condition instantiated at the pair $(w,f(w))$ gives condition 2, and the back condition gives condition 3. Conversely the three conditions say exactly that the graph is a bisimulation.

**Reference.** Blackburn, de Rijke, Venema, Modal Logic (Chapter 2).

### logic:filtration (equivalent)

A filtration of $\mathcal{M}$ through $\Sigma$ is any model $\mathcal{M}^{f}$ on the set of $\equiv_{\Sigma}$-classes such that, for all $w$, the set of formulas of $\Sigma$ true at $[w]$ in $\mathcal{M}^{f}$ equals the set of formulas of $\Sigma$ true at $w$ in $\mathcal{M}$.

**Conditions.** $\Sigma$ finite and closed under subformulas; the equivalence with the three-condition definition holds for any such $\Sigma$.

**Equivalence.** The three conditions are exactly what is needed to run the induction proving that $\Sigma$-formulas are preserved (logic:filtration-lemma.2); conversely, if all $\Sigma$-formulas are preserved, then condition 1 holds (propositional variables are in $\Sigma$), condition 2 holds (if $wRv$ and $w\models\Box B$ with $\Box B\in\Sigma$ then $v\models B$, so $[v]$ is a successor of $[w]$ in any relation satisfying the preservation requirement together with $\Box$-monotonicity), and condition 3 holds because $[w]R^{f}[v]$ and $w\models\Box B$ force $[w]\models\Box B$, hence $[v]\models B$.

**Reference.** Blackburn, de Rijke, Venema, Modal Logic (Chapter 2); Chagrov and Zakharyaschev, Modal Logic (Chapter 5).

### logic:filtration (NOT equivalent)

Variant: dropping condition 3 (keeping only conditions 1 and 2) gives a 'filtration' in a weaker sense.

**Conditions.** Not equivalent: condition 3 is needed for the backward direction of the truth lemma at $\Box$.

**Equivalence.** Without condition 3 the quotient relation may contain extra arrows that make $\Box C$ false at $[w]$ although it is true at $w$; the filtration lemma then fails. The standard fix is to require the truth lemma itself as the definition, which restores equivalence with the three-condition definition.

**Reference.** Blackburn, de Rijke, Venema, Modal Logic (Chapter 2), where the three conditions are stated explicitly.
